name: Vera Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and anything you say is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on commercial policies at a regional insurer, so small business cover: cafés, hair salons, builders, a few corner shops. Most of my day is renewals and changes, like a café adding a new freezer or a builder hiring an apprentice. I check what's changed, update the policy, send out the new documents and answer the phone when the owners get confused. Our office is above a bank on the high street, about twenty of us.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the business owners; they're straight talkers and they remember you. I've had one salon owner send me a cake every Christmas for four years. What's tiring is the renewal rush in spring when everything comes due. I've started using one of the AI tools now and then to summarise a long policy schedule, once I saw a colleague do it without getting into trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say about what I expected, really; it helps with summaries and that's about it. At work I'd shrug. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's fine in this world. A café owner doesn't want a chatbot explaining why the policy won't cover a broken freezer. A café owner wants me on the phone saying what to do next. The bigger worry is at home, because my boyfriend Marco is a self-employed electrician and his work goes up and down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my renewals and keep using the summary tool when it saves time. We'd keep about three months saved and try to push it to four before winter, when Marco's work slows. I might do his invoices on Sunday evenings, like I do now, so he gets paid faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit of the usual money worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How up and down is Marco's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some months he earns twice what I do, and in January he can go three weeks with almost nothing. My salary is the steady one. That's why I can't be relaxed about my job, even when nothing's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if January was bad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways and the second streaming service. We don't spend much on clothes anyway. The car stays, because Marco needs the van and I need my car for the office.

I'd **shrug** at work and post nothing online.

The bigger worry is **Marco's irregular** electrician income.

Push savings from **three to four months** before winter.
Keep doing **Marco's invoices** on Sunday evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change and we'll have to adapt, like every other industry has. I'd tell people at work to learn the tools properly. I'd keep it pretty neutral online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, renewals and policy changes are just the kind of checking work on the card. I think the team of twenty goes to twelve within three years. My boyfriend is an electrician, and for the first time in my life his job looks safer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training on the new tools as soon as they're announced, and ask my manager about moving to underwriting assistant, which needs more judgement. I'd start doing Marco's quotes and scheduling properly, not just invoices, so his business has a real office side. We'd push savings to five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Not panicking, but I'd be watching the noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why underwriting assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone still decides whether to cover a builder who's had three claims in two years. That's judgement and a bit of gut, which I think lasts longer than typing. It's also better paid, by about 3,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marco say about you running his office side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco would love it; he hates paperwork. The only problem is it doesn't pay much yet. It's a backup, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody could have planned for this speed, so let's help each other. I'd be practical with friends: save, don't panic. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my desk job is gone by 2028. Underwriting is thinking work too, so that doesn't save me. Two years is enough time to learn to wire a plug properly, not enough to become an electrician. So I'd become the electrician's office instead, while hands-on work still has about three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending right away and get savings to six months. I'd go full-time with Marco's business as soon as I'm let go, doing quotes, bookings and customers, and push him into EV chargers and solar, where demand would jump. I'd do a short electrical safety course so I can help on site with basic jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. But I'd want to be doing something with my hands that day, not sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office side is thinking work. Wouldn't AI do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, eventually, you're right. But a small electrician with a person answering the phone would still win jobs for a bit. It's not forever, it's three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I honestly don't know. Maybe Marco and I are installing the robots' charging points. I can't plan that far in a world moving that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain if people start now. At work I'd be telling the younger ones to pick a trade or a skill. Online I'd share anything useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the length of an apprenticeship. I'd start one at 28 and finish just before the robots learn to climb ladders. The desk work goes around 2031, the electrical work lasts until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an electrical apprenticeship next year, with Marco as my supervisor, and drop to part-time at the insurer. I'd save hard in the meantime, 250 a month. Once AGI arrived, I'd be working on site full-time with Marco, not behind a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it's the good kind of nervous, like before a driving test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it a strange thing, training under your boyfriend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. We'd have rules, like no arguing about work at dinner. But he's patient and I'd rather learn from him than a stranger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Part-time at the insurer means less pay. Can you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about. Apprentice pay is low, but with half my salary and Marco's work we'd cover rent. We'd skip a holiday or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so nobody should panic. I'd tell friends to keep an eye on it. I'd be pretty calm in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, with ten years I wouldn't rush. I'd watch which of my colleagues land well and copy whoever lands best. I'd be 37 when it comes, which is still young enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer, take any AI training they offer, and keep doing Marco's office side on weekends. I'd look at the apprenticeship again in three or four years, once I see how the first movers do. We'd buy a small house in the next few years while my salary is still solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Watchful rather than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a house now, if things are changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because both our incomes are fine for the next few years and a mortgage is easier to get with a salary. If I wait until I'm retraining, no bank will lend to us. It's the window to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you move faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they stopped hiring on my team, I'd start the apprenticeship that year. That's my signal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to learn a trade properly. Every renewal I handle is a small business betting on next year. I'd quite like to know what my own next year looks like. What would help is apprenticeships for adults that pay enough to live on, not just teenager wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the small businesses I insure. If their customers lose jobs, they lose customers. It's all connected, and nobody talks about that part.

headlineQuote: Every renewal I handle is a small business betting on next year. I'd quite like to know what my own next year looks like.
portrait: Vera, 27, handles **small business policies** at a regional insurer and lives with Marco, a self-employed electrician.
She's **pragmatic**, adopting tools once she sees colleagues use them safely.
Her escape route runs through **Marco's trade**: office side first, apprenticeship later.
She times big moves to signals, like a **hiring freeze** or a mortgage window.
She worries about the **local businesses** she insures as much as herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to **learn a trade** properly.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** that pay enough to live on.
